definition: Exoneration is the official clearing of a person from blame — the accusation shown to be unfounded and the burden of guilt lifted entirely.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word exoneration. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know exoneration should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The audit ended in a one-page exoneration: every receipt accounted for, and the rumor that had trailed the treasurer for a year withdrawn in writing.
A pardon is weaker than an exoneration: it lifts the punishment while the guilt stays on the record — mercy, not correction — whereas an exoneration erases the blame itself.
Rehabilitation goes further than exoneration — after the blame is erased, rehabilitation restores everything it had cost: the rank, the reputation, the name back on the honor roll.

An acquittal is a trial verdict — the jury finds the charge not proven, which may mean innocence or may mean thin evidence. Exoneration is stronger and can come years later: it clears the blame itself, usually because the facts now show the accusation was wrong.

Vindication is the broad word for being proved right — a theory, a warning, a decision can all be vindicated, and no one need have been accused of anything. Exoneration is narrower: someone was blamed for a wrong, and the blame is formally lifted.

For a hundred years the town's histories told the same story: the 1912 courthouse fire had begun in the file room, and the night clerk, Elias Ward, was dismissed for leaving a lamp burning.
Ward denied it until he died, and the blame followed his family for generations.

Then a graduate student cataloguing the county archive found the fire marshal's original notes, missing from every published account: they traced the blaze to a faulty chimney flue two floors above the file room, a defect the county had been warned about twice that winter.
Last spring the council voted unanimously to correct the record.
The town historian called the vote what it was -- a formal exoneration, arriving a century late but complete, the accusation against Ward finally shown to be groundless.
